analysis.one_liner: Gives workers the right to request schedule changes and requires advance notice and pay for last-minute schedule changes.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 102 cosponsors, was referred to four House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let any employee at a company with 15 or more workers ask for changes to their schedule — hours, timing, location, advance notice, or steadier hours — without fear of being fired or punished. Employers would have to discuss the request in good faith and grant it for caregiving, serious illness, education, or a second job unless they had a real business reason not to. It also would have required restaurants, retail, and cleaning employers to pay workers for at least four hours when they show up but get sent home early, pay an extra hour for split shifts or last-minute changes, and post schedules two weeks ahead.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in retail, food service, and cleaning jobs — about 24 million people, most of them women earning around $9 to $11 an hour — plus any employee at larger companies who needs a steadier or more predictable schedule to arrange child care, keep a second job, attend training, or manage a health condition. Low-wage hourly workers with the least schedule control would benefit most.

how_it_helps.text: Any employee could formally request a schedule change for hours, timing, location, notice, or steadier hours, and the employer would have to discuss it in good faith and explain any denial [S2].

Employers would have to grant requests tied to serious health conditions, caregiving, education or training programs, or a part-timer's second job, unless they could show a bona fide business reason [S2].

Retail, food service, and cleaning workers would get at least four hours of pay when they report for work but are sent home early, one hour of pay for split shifts or on-call instructions, and one extra hour of pay for shifts changed with less than 24 hours' notice [S3].
Those workers would receive written schedules and minimum-hour commitments, with 14 days' advance notice before a new schedule takes effect, posted where they can see it [S3].

The bill makes it illegal for employers to retaliate against workers for exercising these rights and allows workers to sue for lost wages, equal liquidated damages, and attorney's fees, with Labor Department enforcement on top [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in retail, food service, and cleaning — restaurants, big-box and other retailers, hotel and building services companies — would bear new scheduling and pay obligations, and any employer with 15 or more employees would face the interactive-process and anti-retaliation requirements. Some of these costs could be passed to consumers through prices or absorbed through leaner scheduling.

drawbacks.text: The scheduling mandates apply only to retail, food service, and cleaning occupations, so many other hourly workers with unstable schedules would get advance-notice and reporting-pay protections only if the Labor Secretary later designates their occupation [S3].

The advance-notice and pay requirements would raise labor costs for low-margin restaurants and retailers, which could respond by hiring fewer people, cutting base hours, or raising prices — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

The bill exempts workers covered by a collective bargaining agreement whose terms govern scheduling, and for routine requests unrelated to caregiving or education, employers may deny for any reason that is not unlawful [S2].
Civil penalties are small — up to $100 for notice violations and $1,100 for retaliation — which critics would say gives employers little reason to comply without vigorous enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — predictable schedules and pay for hours a worker is required to show up or sit by the phone — is real and falls on the country's lowest-paid workers, and it builds in employer flexibility for genuine business needs. The main cost falls on low-margin employers in three industries, and the limits (small penalties, three-industry scope, union exemption) narrow its reach. It is a targeted first step rather than a comprehensive fix, but the trade it asks for is modest.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees, then parked in two subcommittees, and the House never acted on it before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: DeLauro introduced the bill on July 15, 2015, and it was referred to the Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary committees [S5].

On July 29, 2015 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, and on November 16, 2015 to the Education and the Workforce Subcommittee on Workforce Protections [S5].
No committee marked up the bill, no vote was held, and no further action appears in the record before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1].
The bill had 102 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, giving it no apparent path in a Republican-controlled House without a committee hearing or floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retail, restaurant, and cleaning employers are better off: they never had to take on the reporting-time pay, split-shift pay, or two-week advance notice requirements the bill would have imposed. The workers it was written for gained nothing.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: All 102 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans holding the House majority and chairing every committee of referral, the bill never moved.

industries.note: The bill would require reporting-time pay, split-shift pay, extra pay for last-minute changes, and two weeks' advance notice for food preparation and serving workers — the occupation with the most unstable scheduling in the bill's findings (64 percent learn their schedule a week or less in advance).
Retail sales workers would gain the same advance-notice and minimum-pay protections, raising costs for a sector that relies heavily on just-in-time scheduling to match staffing to customer demand.
Janitors, cleaners, and housekeeping staff are covered by the same scheduling and pay requirements, adding cost for building services and hospitality cleaning employers.

industries.industry: Retail and food service sector broadly (as employers of 15 or more)
industries.note: Beyond the scheduling pay rules, all covered employers would gain a defined interactive process for schedule requests and an explicit record that schedule-related denials are lawful when there is a bona fide business reason, which some employers would see as workable structure rather than pure burden.
